title: Accounting for Lawyers

jokes.text: Is the dean planning another ridiculous event, or is the Greendale hat club still struggling to be noteworthy?
jokes.setup: Everyone in the study group is wearing odd hats and Jeff notices
jokes.punchline: The punchline is the framing itself — both options are equally pathetic, with 'struggling to be noteworthy' as the kicker
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff sardonic opener. The binary structure (either/or) works well and 'struggling to be noteworthy' is a nicely precise put-down. Character-integrated — it could only be Jeff's voice.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: If you're talking about it, it must be noteworthy.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: We talk about lots of annoying stuff. That doesn't make it noteworthy.

jokes.text: You're talking about it. / I talk about lots of stuff that annoys me.
jokes.setup: Jeff dismisses the hat club as not noteworthy
jokes.punchline: He's immediately pointed out that he IS talking about it; his retort is that he talks about lots of things that annoy him — which is both a confession and a character statement
jokes.explanation: Quick, tight exchange. Jeff's self-aware smugness is well-captured in the economy of the response. Not groundbreaking but efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Guten Tag, everyone! Welcome to Greendale's Oktoberfest, fo' shizzle!

jokes.text: Guten tag, homies.
jokes.setup: The Dean arrives to announce Oktoberfest
jokes.punchline: His greeting fuses formal German with street slang — the collision is the joke, and it's entirely in character
jokes.explanation: Three words that perfectly encapsulate Dean Pelton's oblivious cultural mashing. Maximum economy. The juxtaposition is absurd but grounded in character — this is exactly who he is.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We don't really celebrate German culture here very often.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Yeah, I wonder why.

jokes.text: It's not often we get to celebrate German culture. / It's not often we want to.
jokes.setup: The Dean enthusiastically promotes Oktoberfest
jokes.punchline: Jeff's dry retort reframes the Dean's celebration as something the community actively avoids
jokes.explanation: Solid sardonic comeback. The parallel structure ('not often we get / not often we want') is clean. Slightly expected from Jeff but lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Welcome everyone to Popktoberfest!

jokes.text: Yeah... a little goes a long way. / True.
jokes.setup: The group is piling on the Dean's German culture enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: The agreement is too casual and complete — 'True.' is delivered with zero pushback, implying shared unspoken consensus that German culture is to be rationed
jokes.explanation: Minor laugh, mostly a tag on the previous joke. The 'True.' agreement is the comedic beat but it's underdeveloped and not very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: We're expanding our horizons, much like Germany in the late 1930s—

jokes.text: 'Pop and locktoberfest.' The central event will be a pop-and-lock-a-thon.
jokes.setup: Dean explains his plan to add 'color' to Oktoberfest by adding a break-dance contest
jokes.punchline: The name 'Pop and Locktoberfest' — the earnest mashup of hip-hop culture with a German beer festival — is the joke. The Dean delivers it with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: The portmanteau itself is funny — it's stupid in a smart way, exactly what Dean Pelton events always are. The concept escalation (Oktoberfest → break-dance) is well-executed and character-perfect. The 'adding color' phrasing also works as a subtle clueless-Dean moment.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: A break-dance contest? I'm in.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, what? No, Jeff, you can't dance.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I've been taking lessons.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: For how long?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Since this morning.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm joining the suicide squad.

jokes.text: Winner gets to annex Poland. Kidding! The winner gets an iTunes gift card.
jokes.setup: The Dean is describing the prize for the pop-and-lock contest
jokes.punchline: He teases a Nazi/WWII reference ('annex Poland') as the prize before revealing the actual prize is a mundane iTunes gift card — the reversal deflates to bathos
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. The dark historical joke lands because it's immediately undercut by the mundane prize reveal — it's both a good dark joke AND a good anti-climax. The structure is clean: big dark setup → 'Kidding!' → pathetic reality. The Dean's oblivious delivery makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We could paint a tunnel on the wall like in cartoons.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That won't work.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Not with that attitude.

jokes.text: What should we name our team? / Okay. I'm gonna go hang myself in my closet. / I'm comin' with.
jokes.setup: The group enthusiastically begins planning for the pop-and-lock contest
jokes.punchline: Jeff responds to the naming question with a suicidal non-sequitur; someone immediately volunteers to join him — the dark joke is doubled by the eager agreement
jokes.explanation: Jeff's nihilism is well-deployed; the 'I'm comin' with' echo sells it. The dark humor is earned through shared disdain for the event. Quick and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You worked with someone. That someone is no longer in your life. Statistically, you either had a falling out, they moved away, or one of you died. Given that you're not depressed, it was probably the first one. You said something inappropriate, they got offended, and now you're pretending it wasn't a big deal.

jokes.text: Is it me, or is this campus getting more cartoonish every day? / Yep. It's exciting.
jokes.setup: Jeff laments the absurdity escalating around them (Oktoberfest, pop-and-lock)
jokes.punchline: Abed enthusiastically agrees that it's exciting — meta-acknowledging that the show itself is getting more cartoonish, and Abed genuinely approves
jokes.explanation: Strongly meta — Abed commenting on the show's own escalating absurdism is pitch-perfect Community. The fact that he LIKES it is what makes the joke resonate. This sets up the tunnel gag that follows.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Jeff, I expected you to be happy to see me. But instead, I'm observing a pronounced downward curvature of your mouth, a contraction of the orbicularis oculi muscles, and a general absence of the zygomatic major activation typically associated with positive emotional states.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You could've just said I don't look happy.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Yes, well, where's the fun in that?

jokes.text: I painted a tunnel on the side of the library. When it dries, I'm going for it.
jokes.setup: Abed has just celebrated the campus becoming more cartoonish
jokes.punchline: He reveals he's literally painted a Looney Tunes-style tunnel on the library wall and plans to run through it — a direct callback to Wile E. Coyote logic, delivered as sincere reportage
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a standout Community moment. The Looney Tunes reference is EARNED as a callback to Abed's 'exciting' comment, delivered with complete deadpan sincerity, and it pays off AGAIN at the episode's end (21:05). Character integration is near-perfect — only Abed would do this, only Abed would say this, only Abed would believe it. Economy is flawless. The setup/callback structure across the whole episode elevates it further.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, you worked with Alan?

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Different Alan. We were partners on a case in '09.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So you're saying you two are like Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid?

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: No, Butch and Sundance worked together. We worked with different partners—like they did with other outlaws.

jokes.text: The one wearing the Gucci suit and the lightweight woven wool-mohair blend?
jokes.setup: Jeff spots an old colleague and points him out to the group
jokes.punchline: His identification of a person in a crowd is entirely by fashion label — which reveals more about Jeff's own obsessions than it describes Alan
jokes.explanation: Good character-comedy. The specificity of 'lightweight woven wool-mohair blend' is funny precisely because it's too specific — it's how Jeff's brain works. Character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, I'm not actually a teacher here. I'm just a student.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh my God. That's somehow even more embarrassing.

jokes.text: This is all I need. / Excuse me, sir. You're all my friend needs.
jokes.setup: Jeff spots Alan and doesn't want to be introduced — he's embarrassed by the group
jokes.punchline: Before he can protest, someone in the group immediately calls Alan over on his behalf, exposing Jeff's context
jokes.explanation: Functional group dynamics joke. The irony of Jeff's social anxiety being immediately violated by his friends is well-timed but not especially original.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: I wasn't at yoga. I was at Narcotics Anonymous.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: I lied about the yoga thing.

jokes.text: Your mouth isn't curved upwards. Did I misread something?
jokes.setup: Alan approaches Jeff's group and can see Jeff is uncomfortable
jokes.punchline: Instead of acknowledging the awkwardness directly, Alan describes Jeff's facial expression like a clinical observation — 'mouth not curved upwards' as an overly precise description of a frown
jokes.explanation: Smart joke. The clinical over-description of a frown ('mouth isn't curved upwards') is an unusual comedic lens and suits a lawyer's literal, strategic mind. Good character work for a first-appearance character.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We're like lawyers, except we actually put the trash back on the streets.

jokes.text: Tango? / Sundance. We worked with different partners.
jokes.setup: Alan tests an old nickname on Jeff
jokes.punchline: Jeff corrects him — but the correction reveals they were BOTH running buddy-movie-style schemes with DIFFERENT partners, making both of them simultaneously less cool and funnier
jokes.explanation: Economical and clever. The buddy-movie nickname subversion works because both options (Tango and Sundance) reveal ego, and the 'different partners' explanation is a funny deflation.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: I quit cocaine, not my lifestyle.

jokes.text: Wait. That's worse than the truth. / I'm a student.
jokes.setup: Jeff tells Alan he's a teacher at Greendale
jokes.punchline: Alan's reaction — 'that's worse than the truth' — precedes Jeff's correction that he's actually a student, which is both the worse truth AND a funnier escalation
jokes.explanation: Very well-structured two-step. Alan's 'that's worse than the truth' anticipates the reveal and frames it perfectly — teacher is bad, student is worse. The structure creates escalation through delay.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: What has Greendale done to you? Look at you! You're wearing cargo pants!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: They're practical.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: They're a cry for help.

jokes.text: Remember when you asked for my secret, I said yoga? I lied.
jokes.setup: Alan says he's at Greendale for an N.A. meeting — implying drug addiction
jokes.punchline: He casually admits he had previously lied about his wellness secret being yoga, as if that's a reasonable disclosure to make to an old colleague you're meeting on the street
jokes.explanation: Good delivery of an overshare. The 'I lied' kicker is delivered with exactly the wrong tone (casual, unbothered) for the gravity of what he's disclosing. Economical and character-revealing.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You have no idea what Greendale has done to you.

dialogue.speaker: Hat Club Member
dialogue.line: Hey Alan, hat club meeting in five!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Case in point.

jokes.text: I quit doing blow, not being rad.
jokes.setup: Jeff wonders if Alan is allowed to get a drink
jokes.punchline: 'I quit doing blow, not being rad' — the casual admission of cocaine use as the thing he gave up, contrasted with the preservation of his self-image as 'rad'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The parallel construction is perfect: 'blow / rad' — the juxtaposition of a serious drug addiction with the casual bro-ism of 'being rad' is both funny and character-defining. Maximum economy (seven words). The word 'rad' is doing enormous work. This is the kind of line that gets quoted.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Did you hear? Jeff Winger is apparently dating someone from the air conditioning repair annex.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: That's not really news, Chang.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Well, it is to me!

jokes.text: D.A. called us the litterbugs — we put so much trash back out on those streets.
jokes.setup: Jeff is bragging to Abed about his and Alan's legal prowess.
jokes.punchline: The nickname 'litterbugs' reframes getting criminals acquitted as environmental pollution — 'trash back out on the streets.' Jeff delivers this as a brag, not an admission of moral failure.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever wordplay with moral darkness underneath. 'Litterbugs' is a perfect double meaning — they litter the streets with criminals — and Jeff's pride in the nickname reveals his pre-Greendale amorality. Very character-integrated and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not funny. That's Johnny Carson.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Jon Stewart.

jokes.text: Well, those cargo pants would suggest otherwise.
jokes.setup: Someone tries to prevent Jeff from leaving for a drink by reminding him he has class
jokes.punchline: Alan undermines Jeff's student status by pointing to cargo pants as evidence he doesn't belong in class — the fashion insult is exactly the kind of snob-code Alan and Jeff share
jokes.explanation: Sharp and efficient. The cargo pants as class marker is a good specific comedic vehicle. Alan immediately speaks Jeff's language (fashion snobbery) which reveals their bond while being funny.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Jon Stewart? That's your comedy reference? Man, that makes me feel old.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You're not old.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: No, I mean it makes me feel like I'm old. Like, that's how I know I'm getting older—when the things that were current when I was young are now what young people reference as 'classic.'

jokes.text: What has this place done to you? / Hat club! / Now you have some idea.
jokes.setup: Alan laments what community college has done to Jeff
jokes.punchline: The Dean happens to pass by yelling 'Hat club!' at exactly the right moment to perfectly illustrate Alan's concern — Jeff's resigned 'Now you have some idea' is the button
jokes.explanation: Structurally excellent. The comedic timing here is near-perfect — the Dean's 'Hat club!' is a visual/aural punchline that arrives exactly when needed, without setup. Jeff's 'Now you have some idea' as resignation rather than explanation is deadpan gold. The scene essentially writes itself into a perfect moment. This is craft-level sitcom architecture.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm not gonna rip off my exit.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: *walks out with exaggerated sound effects*

jokes.text: Word has it on campus that Winger's too busy hanging out with his cool new lawyer friend.
jokes.setup: The study group is planning the pop-and-lock team
jokes.punchline: Treating Jeff's social life as campus news — 'word has it on campus' applied to something mundane — satirizes both the insular community college world and Jeff's perceived celebrity status
jokes.explanation: Functional observational joke about Greendale's small-pond dynamics. Not particularly sharp but serves the plot.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: They're so close, they're practically attached at the hip.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Actually, more like attached at the cell phone holster.

jokes.text: That's your Carson? / Jon Stewart. / You depress me.
jokes.setup: Someone asks Troy to do his celebrity impression to demonstrate his charisma for the pop-and-lock team
jokes.punchline: Troy's Carson is Jon Stewart — meaning his reference point for 'classic showbiz' is a cable political comedian; the other person is depressed by the generational gap
jokes.explanation: Smart generational joke. The gap between Johnny Carson and Jon Stewart as 'the same kind of thing' is a good comedic premise. 'You depress me' is the right amount of dramatic response.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's like when in Inception, they keep going deeper into dreams and losing track of reality. Alan's got us all in a nested conversation about whether we're even having the conversation we think we're having.

jokes.text: And don't rip off this exit. / Shoom, shoom.
jokes.setup: A rival pop-and-lock team warns Troy not to copy their exit
jokes.punchline: Troy immediately does the exact exit move ('Shoom, shoom') the moment they're gone — the audience infers a very specific comedic spin move that is exactly what was warned against
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy inferred from dialogue. The beat works because the prohibition is immediately violated; the 'shoom, shoom' sound-effect implies the move was both worth warning about and immediately copied.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Wait, you actually saw that movie?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I made that reference assuming no one would get it.

jokes.text: Those two are like siamese twins attached at the cell phone holster.
jokes.setup: The group laments Jeff's absence from study group due to Alan
jokes.punchline: The 'cell phone holster' as the shared appendage — not hip, not heart, but the most specific symbol of their professional/bro identity
jokes.explanation: Good metaphor. 'Cell phone holster' as the specific object of attachment is a smart, specific choice — it immediately characterizes both men as a certain type of guy.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Has anyone been injured at work?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, one time I was working on a shrimp boat off the coast of Louisiana, and I got my arm caught in the winch. The captain had to choose between cutting off my arm or sinking the boat. He chose to sink the boat.

jokes.text: Our concern is that Alan is to Jeff what Rob Lowe was to James Spader in the 1990 film 'Bad Influence.' He's a bad influence.
jokes.setup: The group discusses Alan's hold over Jeff
jokes.punchline: Abed explains the entire dynamic through a film reference, then explains the reference ('He's a bad influence') as if the group might not catch the title/theme
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed. The film reference is specific (a 1990 B-thriller most people haven't seen), the explanation of the reference reveals he knows the audience might not get it, and his deadpan delivery of 'He's a bad influence' as if summarizing in case the metaphor was too subtle is perfect. Character integration is near-maximum — this is exactly and only Abed.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So in Christianity, you can be forgiven for anything, right?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Well, yes, if you truly repent.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So if I murdered someone, I could be forgiven?

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Yes, but—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Then why do you always get mad when I'm late?

jokes.text: Mmm, or any bar.
jokes.setup: Jeff says he and Alan are going to take a 'quick sidebar'
jokes.punchline: Britta spots and delivers the legal pun — 'sidebar' means a legal conference, but Alan is at N.A. and they're clearly going drinking — 'any bar' completes the pun
jokes.explanation: Clean wordplay. 'Or any bar' is an efficient pun on 'sidebar' that earns its laugh. Britta's delivery as a dry correction gives it the right understated energy.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: You know, Jeff, your manipulation skills are really something special.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Thanks, Alan. I've been practicing.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: In fact, I picture you as a trophy on my shelf, doing mind games to a brain.

jokes.text: Oh, he's got Britta down!
jokes.setup: Britta delivers a dry pun/observation
jokes.punchline: Troy's excited reaction — treating Britta's dry sarcasm as an impression Alan is doing — is a funny misread that reveals Troy's affectionate confusion about Britta's personality
jokes.explanation: Good quick reaction beat. Troy misreads the entire interaction (thinking Alan is performing an impression) which is both funny and characterful — his enthusiasm for the wrong interpretation is very Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: See, if I just lean in like this and make eye contact, you'll feel compelled to agree with me.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Get away from me!

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: *throws punch*

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: I'm calling my lawyer. That's assault!

jokes.text: Have you or someone you know been injured at work? / Yes! A shrimp boat ran over my cousin.
jokes.setup: Alan turns to the group and delivers a mock personal injury ad pitch
jokes.punchline: Shirley's immediate earnest response about her shrimp-boat-injured cousin is both a perfect Shirley character moment AND a Forrest Gump reference, delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Funny on two levels. Alan's personal injury ad bit is a good character entrance, but Shirley's shrimp boat response — a Forrest Gump reference smuggled into genuine sincerity — doubles the laugh. The best part is that Alan has to take it seriously: 'That's serious. Call me.' Perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm not bald. I'm follicle-challenged.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: It's a medical condition. Very rare. Very biblical.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm like Moses. He parted the Red Sea. I parted my hair. With my mind.

jokes.text: Shirley, if I killed a man, as a Christian, would you forgive me? / I would. / Then either that man's life is worth less than your time, or it's okay for me to be late.
jokes.setup: Shirley demands that Jeff be more respectful of the group's time
jokes.punchline: Jeff constructs an elaborate logical trap using Shirley's Christian forgiveness to dismiss her complaint — the false syllogism is delivered with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. Jeff's manipulation-via-logic is a core character trait, and this is a textbook example of it deployed brilliantly. The setup (asking if she'd forgive murder) lures Shirley into her Christian virtue, and then the logical trap snaps shut. The structure is tight, the character integration is perfect (only Jeff does this), and 'Ha ha! No!' from Shirley is the ideal button — she knows she was had but can't argue the logic. Comparable in craft to the vasectomy anchor example.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Jeff, you've committed fraud, you've tampered with evidence, you've obstructed justice, you've impersonated a lawyer...

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, where is this going?

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: In any normal profession, these would be disqualifying. But in law? These are the traits we admire. You're going to fit right in.

jokes.text: If they gave away awards for mind games, the statue'd be Jeff Winger doing it to a brain.
jokes.setup: Alan watches Jeff's manipulation of Shirley
jokes.punchline: The award metaphor escalates into a surreal visual — the trophy itself would be Jeff's likeness performing mind games on a brain sculpture — the image is both specific and ridiculous
jokes.explanation: Vivid and original. The specific visual of a Jeff Winger trophy doing mind games on a brain is inventively strange. Alan's admiration is delivered with lawyer-bro enthusiasm that fits his character.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: So Jeff and Alan walk into a bar, and... and the bartender says, 'Why the long... uh... why are you two so... together?' Get it? Because they're... they're like... they do things... together.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Troy, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm trying to make a joke about you guys being... you know... intimate. Like, sexually. That's what I was going for.

jokes.text: Come on, Jeff's bush league. I gave seminars on manipulation. I could reach into a man's soul and unravel it with one tug.
jokes.setup: Alan praises Jeff's mind games
jokes.punchline: He immediately one-ups Jeff by claiming his own manipulation skills are seminar-worthy and can literally unravel souls — the boast is so over-the-top it becomes comedic, especially from someone at an N.A. meeting
jokes.explanation: 'Unravel it with one tug' is a vivid image that earns the laugh. The setup of calling Jeff 'bush league' works as competitive lawyer posturing.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, I know you from somewhere.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: I don't think so.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: No, I definitely do. Oh! You were at Greendale!

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: I was?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Yes! You were in my Psych class. But I can't tell you anything about that because of student confidentiality. Actually, you failed the final.

jokes.text: Cool. Hit me. / You're bald. / So are you. / I'll kill you, you... / Mistrial.
jokes.setup: Jeff dares Alan to demonstrate his soul-unraveling manipulation on him
jokes.punchline: Alan's 'manipulation' is just 'you're bald' — it immediately triggers Alan himself (who is also bald) — the escalation collapses into rage and Jeff calls 'Mistrial' as a legal non-sequitur to end it
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly structured. The setup (Alan claims he can unravel any soul) makes the collapse funnier — his 'move' is a playground taunt that boomerangs immediately. 'So are you' is perfect, 'Mistrial' as the legal escape hatch is both in-character and an ideal button. Five words total do enormous structural work. Very high economy.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You went from annoying to insufferable. That's called character development.

jokes.text: You're bald. / So are you. / I'll kill you, you... / Come here! / Mistrial.
jokes.setup: Alan attempts his soul-unraveling technique on Pierce.
jokes.punchline: His devastating insight is simply 'You're bald' — Pierce is so instantly enraged by this that he attacks Alan. Jeff's legal term 'Mistrial' as a de-escalation word is the topper.
jokes.explanation: Excellent multi-layer joke. The setup promises sophisticated psychological insight; the delivery is 'You're bald' — maximum deflation of Alan's grandiosity. Pierce's hair insecurity (a known character trait) makes it perfectly targeted. 'So are you' as Pierce's comeback is the logical counter but it doesn't save him. 'Mistrial' as Jeff's intervention is the perfect legal word repurposed for a physical altercation — and it's funny that it apparently works. Very high character integration across all three characters.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We could play charades to guess the secret!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: If we played charades, people would pay to watch us.

jokes.text: I have hair. (Talking head confession, delivered to camera)
jokes.setup: The bald exchange between Jeff and Alan
jokes.punchline: Jeff's isolated talking-head: 'I have hair.' delivered with complete earnest defensiveness, as if the camera needed to know
jokes.explanation: Three words, enormous laugh. The confessional format amplifies the vanity — Jeff felt so stung by the bald accusation that he needed the documentary record corrected. The seriousness of the declaration ('I have hair. / Father, I have hair.') against the smallness of the concern is pitch-perfect. 'Father, I have hair' as a solemn declaration is especially absurd. Economy score is a 10 — there is no way to do more with fewer words.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: It's a movie!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: It's... it's 'Inception'!

jokes.text: Father, I have hair. On a tax evasion case.
jokes.setup: Jeff's 'I have hair' confessional continues
jokes.punchline: He adds 'Father, I have hair' as if speaking to God or a priest, then the scene cuts to him saying it in context — apparently he said this phrase during a tax evasion case — the absurdity of the context is the punchline
jokes.explanation: The expansion of the 'I have hair' bit into a tax evasion case context is brilliantly absurd. 'Father, I have hair' as a courtroom non-sequitur implies Jeff's vanity intruded into a legal proceeding, which is a perfect character revelation. The escalation from private confession to courtroom utterance is unexpected and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What? I'm not gonna tell anyone. Besides, half those people are just there because they got a DUI. They're not real addicts.

jokes.text: Jeff, you know what lawyers call someone who defrauds the state bar, cheats on his SATs, and cons his way into a firm? / Best...Lawyer...Ever.
jokes.setup: Alan seems to be setting up a condemnation of Jeff's past legal misconduct
jokes.punchline: The expected insult reverses into the highest possible professional compliment — the same actions that should disqualify are reframed as skills
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection. The list of Jeff's transgressions is delivered with the cadence of an indictment, so the reversal to 'Best Lawyer Ever' earns a solid laugh. The moral inversion ('cons = skills') is appropriately dark and character-grounded for the law world Community is satirizing.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Frank Zappa

jokes.text: What does Alan have that we don't? / A butt for Jeff's Weiner.
jokes.setup: The group laments Jeff's preference for Alan's company
jokes.punchline: The blunt anatomical suggestion that Jeff and Alan have a sexual dynamic — using 'Weiner' (Jeff's surname) for the double entendre
jokes.explanation: Decent crude pun using Jeff's surname. The quick clarification exchange ('I mean, we all have butts... I'm trying to say they're gay') is funnier than the initial line because of the fumbling attempt to explain it.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You guys are talking crazy. This is like when the kids on Blue's Clues think the dog actually knows where things are. You're connecting dots that aren't there.

jokes.text: I mean, we all have butts too. We have butts. Just not for the same thi... / I'm trying to say they're gay.
jokes.setup: The character tries to explain/backpedal the Jeff/Alan sexual joke
jokes.punchline: The increasingly tangled clarification collapses into a blunt 'I'm trying to say they're gay' — the fumbled explanation is funnier than just saying it directly
jokes.explanation: The stumbling self-correction is the joke — it's cringe-adjacent. The clarification 'just not for the same thi...' trailing off before the blunt reset works well structurally.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Give me another one. I need more conspiracy theories.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Go-Gurt is just yogurt.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not a conspiracy theory, that's just a fact.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Exactly.

jokes.text: It's a gateway to narcotics. / Narcotics! I know how I know Alan!
jokes.setup: Shirley moralizes about drinking being a gateway drug; Annie suddenly has a realization
jokes.punchline: Shirley's moralizing accidentally triggers Annie's memory — a great comic non-sequitur where the word 'narcotics' is both Shirley's sermon and Annie's eureka moment
jokes.explanation: Very well-constructed comedic beat. Shirley's morality speech is interrupted by its own language triggering a plot reveal — the structure is tight and both characters are perfect in their roles.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I need my old life back. You know what my current life is? It's like being a tiger in a zoo. Everyone's watching, everyone's got opinions about what I should be doing, and I'm pacing back and forth in a space that's way too small for me.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Except instead of a tiger, I'm a guy in his thirties, and instead of a zoo, it's Greendale Community College surrounded by people who think they know what's best for me.

jokes.text: But I'm not allowed to say. / Which means that you met him in narcotics anonymous.
jokes.setup: Annie says she knows something bad about Alan but can't say it
jokes.punchline: Someone immediately deduces the exact context from the 'can't say' rule — the N.A. confidentiality rule is instantly transparent, defeating its own purpose
jokes.explanation: Good logic joke — the confidentiality reveal defeats itself. Economically told.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: So what you're saying is that you slept with her?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not saying that I did or didn't do anything. What I am saying is that any activities that may or may not have occurred were entirely consensual and happened in a time and place that cannot be definitively proven.

jokes.text: Why bring it up if you're not allowed?
jokes.setup: Annie keeps hinting at the secret she can't share
jokes.punchline: The entirely reasonable question exposes Annie's attention-seeking — she's using the secret as social currency while technically maintaining confidentiality
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical observation that punctures Annie's behavior. Character-specific for Britta (the designated skeptic).

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: If we win this dance contest, Chang gets to join the study group? That's like saying if we win the lottery, we have to give all our money to a guy we met at the bus station who smells like old milk and regret.

jokes.text: Okay. You've gone from precious to annoying.
jokes.setup: Annie keeps teasing the secret in increasingly complicated ways
jokes.punchline: 'Precious to annoying' as a development arc — the phrasing is so specifically condescending that it's funny
jokes.explanation: Very quotable put-down. The progression from 'precious' to 'annoying' as a described character arc is a fresh way to deliver a dismissal.

dialogue.speaker: Ted
dialogue.line: Look, I know it's weird. I have a hole in my hand. But if I were you guys, I'd totally gossip about it too.

jokes.text: What if you don't say it out loud but we guess? / Like charades? / With this group? / I'm watching.
jokes.setup: Someone suggests guessing the secret via charades
jokes.punchline: Abed's 'With this group?' expresses meta-skepticism about the group's charades ability — then Annie's 'I'm watching' positions her as the performer, implying the group IS going to do this
jokes.explanation: Good quick exchange. Abed's 'With this group?' is a moment of self-aware commentary, and Annie's pivot to performer mode is charming.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Wait, Ted uses his weird hand as a power move? He just... flaunts it?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's what I'm saying. Most people would hide it, but Ted? He leans into it.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: That's actually kind of genius. He's weaponized his own deformity.

jokes.text: Four words. / 'Alan got Jeff disbarred.'
jokes.setup: Annie acts out the secret in charades
jokes.punchline: Someone guesses it immediately and correctly on the first try — the entire charades exercise was pointless because they're just saying it anyway
jokes.explanation: Smart anticlimactic structure. The whole 'charades so we don't say it out loud' scheme collapses immediately when someone just says it. The game's pointlessness is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: This place has a real toxic atmosphere. You can feel the moral decay in the air.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I'm talking about my gas. I had the mozzarella sticks from the food court.

jokes.text: Oh, please, those junkies weren't thinking about rules when they were shooting up scag.
jokes.setup: Someone defends N.A. confidentiality rules
jokes.punchline: Pierce's dismissive characterization of N.A. members as 'junkies shooting up scag' — the casually offensive framing is entirely Pierce, and 'scag' as the specific drug term is a funny period-appropriate word choice
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce — casually offensive, using out-of-date drug terminology. The humor is in the character's obliviousness rather than the content of the insult. 'Scag' is doing a lot of work.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Hey guys, what are you—

dialogue.speaker: Study Group
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Hmm. But he's like way too primo for that, Frank Zappa.
jokes.setup: Someone suggests Alan turned Jeff in
jokes.punchline: Pierce's 'Frank Zappa' as a random exclamation — apparently a verbal tic or expression — is baffling and funny precisely because it's unexplained
jokes.explanation: Pierce non-sequiturs are a Community staple. 'Frank Zappa' as a random celebrity exclamation is in-character for Pierce's generational oddness, though somewhat underdeveloped.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: What's Alan's office number?

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: It's 69.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh... oh no.

jokes.text: I know they never covered this on 'Yo, Gabba Gabba,' but that's called circumstantial.
jokes.setup: Annie presents her case that Alan betrayed Jeff
jokes.punchline: Jeff dismisses Annie's theory by implying she's too young/naive to understand the concept of circumstantial evidence, referencing a toddler TV show
jokes.explanation: Jeff's condescension toward Annie's youth is well-deployed here. 'Yo, Gabba Gabba' as the reference is funny because it's a real kids' show and the specificity elevates it above a generic 'you're young' dismissal.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'd like to make an appointment with the doctor.

dialogue.speaker: Ted
dialogue.line: Well, the doctor is in. And he's going to need both of your balls.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Excuse me?

dialogue.speaker: Ted
dialogue.line: For the examination. I'm going to eat them. While you watch. And then I'm going to wear your skin like a tuxedo and seduce your father.

jokes.text: Yes. Did you know that Go-Gurt is just yogurt?
jokes.setup: Jeff asks if anyone else has 'meaningless conspiracy theories'
jokes.punchline: Annie responds with 'Go-Gurt is just yogurt' — a perfectly sincere anti-revelation that is both meaningless and weirdly resonant as a 'conspiracy'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The absurdity is perfectly calibrated — Annie's 'conspiracy theory' is factually true but entirely pointless, which makes it funnier than a fake conspiracy. 'Go-Gurt is just yogurt' is quotable and genuinely surprising. The delivery context (Jeff dismissing 'meaningless theories') makes the response a perfect misfire. High economy — six words do everything.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Does anyone even care about this stupid contest?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'm here to check in. Chang. That's C-H-A-N-G.

jokes.text: You know what a therapist calls this kind of a relationship, right? / A gold mine. / Codependent.
jokes.setup: Britta implies she's about to deliver therapist wisdom about Jeff's relationship with Alan
jokes.punchline: Someone preemptively guesses 'a gold mine' (from the therapist's perspective) before Britta delivers the correct answer 'codependent' — the cynical interpretation of therapy as a business undercuts Britta's earnestness
jokes.explanation: Smart misdirection. 'A gold mine' as the cynical guess reframes therapy as a financial relationship before Britta corrects it. It also reveals Britta's earnestness about psychology as slightly naive.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I've got the supplies for the caper. Rope, duct tape, chloroform... I've tested the chloroform.

jokes.text: I used to run full-speed through the boundless wilderness, and now I'm in the zoo where the horizon is wallpaper and the air is stale and nothing is ever at stake.
jokes.setup: Jeff is explaining why he wants to reconnect with his lawyer life
jokes.punchline: The elaborate metaphor about being an animal in a zoo — applied to Greendale — is funny because of its absurd grandiosity, but also because Jeff's 'boundless wilderness' was apparently just being a sleazy lawyer
jokes.explanation: The metaphor is vivid and the irony is good (Jeff's 'freedom' was lawyerly manipulation), though it runs a bit long for a pure laugh. More dramatic than comic.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Annie, you should be the lookout because if a cop stops us, he's way more likely to let us go if you're here.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's... actually a fair point.

jokes.text: In other words, we're not cool. / I never said that. You may have heard it. I may have thought it, and it may be true. But I never said it.
jokes.setup: Someone summarizes Jeff's speech as 'you're not cool'
jokes.punchline: Jeff's layered non-denial ('never said it / may have heard it / may have thought it / may be true') is a masterclass in technically-not-lying — a lawyer's precision deployed for social cruelty
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. Jeff's escalating non-denial ('you may have heard it / I may have thought it / it may be true') is structurally perfect — each step tightens the trap while maintaining technical innocence. This is EXACTLY Jeff Winger: a lawyer using precision language to be cruel while maintaining deniability. Only he delivers this. Among the episode's best.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, I'm the one who always gets us into this stuff, aren't I? I'm like the catalyst for all of your insane plans.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You know what? I hope this fails. I hope we all get caught and have to face the consequences like adults for once!

jokes.text: No, Abed, I'm going to a cool party at my cool former law firm from when my life was cool.
jokes.setup: Abed asks if Jeff will be at the pop-and-lock-a-thon
jokes.punchline: Jeff's triple use of 'cool' is pathetically over-insistent — protesting too much about how cool everything is reveals the opposite
jokes.explanation: Jeff's self-awareness collapses here in a funny way. The triple 'cool' as insistence is a good self-undermining verbal tic.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: What did Annie say?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I wasn't really listening, but I'm pretty sure she said 'penetrate.'

jokes.text: Fine. You can be on the team. / New deal. If we win, I get to be in the study group.
jokes.setup: The rival pop-and-lock team offers a spot in exchange for something
jokes.punchline: The counteroffer reframes the pop-and-lock competition as a proxy for something much more personal — study group membership — implying the rival has been maneuvering for social access the whole time
jokes.explanation: Decent escalation. The idea that someone would negotiate study group membership through a pop-and-lock contest is appropriately Greendale-absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I became a lawyer because I saw how successful they were. The cars, the suits, the respect - that's what I wanted. Not justice. Not helping people. The money and the image. That's it.

jokes.text: The stakes have never been higher.
jokes.setup: The rival's offer of study group membership in exchange for a pop-and-lock victory
jokes.punchline: The deadpan declaration 'The stakes have never been higher' applied to a break-dance competition at a community college — the epic framing against the mundane stakes
jokes.explanation: Perfect bathetic delivery. The gap between epic declaration and community college break-dance contest is the joke. If this is Abed delivering it, it's even better — he would mean it completely.

dialogue.speaker: Ted
dialogue.line: You know what, Jeff? You inspire me. You make me want to be a worse man.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's... not a compliment.

dialogue.speaker: Ted
dialogue.line: No, no, I mean it. Watching you cut corners, manipulate people, dodge responsibility... it's liberating. You've shown me that being terrible is actually easier and more rewarding.

jokes.text: I had a dream that one day I'd be head of a firm so nobody would be able to talk about the big, weird hole in my hand.
jokes.setup: Ted, the law firm head, gives a toast at the office party
jokes.punchline: His entire dream of professional achievement is revealed to be motivated by silencing commentary about a physical anomaly on his hand — the hole in his hand is both funny and inexplicably specific
jokes.explanation: Excellent comedic introduction for Ted. The 'hole in my hand' is never explained, described, or resolved — it just exists as an absurd character detail delivered with complete sincerity during what should be an inspiring speech. The specificity ('big, weird hole') elevates it. Very strong first appearance joke.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: I have a sexual arrangement with the beach house owner for access to the beach house.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Prostitution: the newest profession.

jokes.text: I know everybody talks about it behind my back, and that's okay. You know, I would.
jokes.setup: Ted continues addressing the hand
jokes.punchline: 'I would' — Ted's self-aware acknowledgment that the hole is objectively worth discussing, without self-pity, is a perfect deadpan
jokes.explanation: The 'I would' is delivered as complete matter-of-fact acceptance that the hole is gossip-worthy. The lack of defensiveness makes it funnier than defensiveness would have. Good callback to the hole setup.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I'm gonna sue somebody!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Shirley, you can't sue everyone. Besides, strippers are already life's victims.

jokes.text: Anyone else with that hand would wear a glove. He controls a room with it.
jokes.setup: Jeff watches Ted work the party with his holey hand
jokes.punchline: 'He controls a room with it' — the admission that Ted has weaponized his deformity into power, which is simultaneously absurd and genuinely admiring
jokes.explanation: The progression from 'hole in hand' absurdity to Jeff's genuine admiration for Ted's mastery is a funny arc. 'He controls a room with it' as admiring analysis of a hand hole is exactly Jeff's character — he respects power above all else.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Did you know that in some parts of the world, human hunting is actually legal? Yeah, it's true. You should really look into it if you're planning a trip.

jokes.text: Oh, um... Hey, when you talk to him, will you mention me? He keeps passing me over for partner.
jokes.setup: Alan invited Jeff to the party, supposedly as an act of friendship
jokes.punchline: He immediately reveals his ulterior motive — using Jeff to lobby for his partnership — before Jeff even has to wonder why he was invited
jokes.explanation: Good reveal of Alan's true motivation. The quickness of the confession (Jeff barely needs to ask) is the comedic beat — Alan has zero shame about using Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I can't even hide behind a pop culture reference for this one.

jokes.text: Alan, did you invite me here with an ulterior motive?
jokes.setup: Alan just confessed his real reason for inviting Jeff
jokes.punchline: Jeff's question is asked AFTER Alan has already admitted it — the deadpan timing implies Jeff either wasn't listening or is performing mock-surprise
jokes.explanation: Minor joke — the comedic beat is in the unnecessary question that answers itself. Light but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, oh my god, oh my god! I chloroformed someone! I chloroformed someone! What is wrong with me?! I'm a bad person! I'm a chloroform person! My life is over! I'm going to jail! I'm going to be someone's prison wife! And not in a fun way!

jokes.text: God, it's a sea of Wingers. This whole place reeks of moral ambiguity. / Actually, that was me. I apologize.
jokes.setup: Britta surveys the law firm party full of slick lawyers
jokes.punchline: Pierce mishears (or willfully interprets) Britta's moral condemnation of the room as a comment about a smell — and apologizes for it
jokes.explanation: Excellent Pierce joke. 'Actually, that was me. I apologize.' works on multiple levels: it mistakes the metaphorical (moral ambiguity) for the literal (a smell), it implies Pierce is emitting an odor, AND his casual apology for the odor is perfect character comedy. The structure is clean, the character integration is high, and the punchline is both surprising and inevitable in retrospect.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Okay, here's what we tell them. We were all chloroformed. Together. By someone else.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, that's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Do you have a better idea?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Actually, I kind of like it.

jokes.text: Now, you guys are new to high society, so just... follow my lead, everything will be fine.
jokes.setup: Jeff's study group has crashed his law firm party
jokes.punchline: Jeff's protective instinct frames himself as a 'high society' guide — the irony being that he's a disbarred community college student
jokes.explanation: Functional irony — Jeff presenting himself as the guide to high society while being a community college student is the implicit joke. Not particularly sharp but serves the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We need to leave. Now. Like, immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Annie just told the Dean that we were at a... a thing. A thing that definitely didn't happen.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: And he believed exactly none of it.

jokes.text: First, why are you here? Second, I don't care. Leave.
jokes.setup: Jeff's study group appears at the law firm party
jokes.punchline: The two-step of 'First... Second...' creates expectation of a measured response, then immediately short-circuits with 'I don't care. Leave.' — the structure promises more than it delivers on purpose
jokes.explanation: Very well-structured short joke. 'First... Second, I don't care' subverts the analytical framework with impatient dismissal. Jeff's voice is perfectly captured in the economy.

dialogue.speaker: Announcer
dialogue.line: Ladies and gentlemen, we are witnessing an unprecedented display of raw athleticism and unbridled passion. Chang moves with the grace of a gazelle, the power of a charging rhino, and the coordination of a newborn giraffe.

dialogue.speaker: Announcer
dialogue.line: What we're seeing here is either the birth of a new dance movement or a man having a severe medical episode. The judges are... confused.

dialogue.speaker: Announcer
dialogue.line: In any case, that's just Chang.

jokes.text: To apologize to you for casting aspersions on your friend. / And to show you we can be cool.
jokes.setup: Jeff demands an explanation for why the group crashed the party
jokes.punchline: Their explanation — 'to show you we can be cool' — directly admits to the insecurity Jeff identified, making them exactly as uncool as he feared
jokes.explanation: Good self-undermining beat. The group's attempt to prove their coolness by showing up uninvited is perfectly anti-cool.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I had to explicitly tell Pierce not to hunt humans.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: And you know what? That was badass.

jokes.text: Fourth floor. 470. / First he said it was 69. / I wanna rub Purell on my brain.
jokes.setup: Annie reports Alan's office number after getting it from him
jokes.punchline: The revelation that Alan's first offered number was 69 — the implication being it was a crude flirtation — followed by the 'Purell on my brain' response (wanting to sanitize the knowledge from one's mind)
jokes.explanation: 'I wanna rub Purell on my brain' is a highly quotable, original expression of mental contamination. The '69' setup is crude but efficient, and the Purell line elevates it into a fresh image.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I see it. Alan betrayed me. But you know what? I still respect his work. The man's a professional.

jokes.text: If we had five guys around here with your balls, we wouldn't need 30 lawyers. / True. But we'd need a good doctor.
jokes.setup: Ted compliments Jeff's nerve ('balls') in a business metaphor
jokes.punchline: Jeff redirects the metaphor to its literal anatomical meaning — 15 sets of testicles would require medical attention
jokes.explanation: Classic literal-pun subversion. The 'you'd need a good doctor' follow-through on the anatomical math is a good quick joke. Jeff's comfort in this world is shown through his quickness.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: He's going to die alone.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm going to dance.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Exactly.

jokes.text: Ted, stop hittin' on my date. / Ha ha ha ha ha! / I'm kidding. We can share. / I get the head! / I love the brain in there! Arr, arr, arr!
jokes.setup: Jeff deflects Ted's attention from something/someone
jokes.punchline: Ted's escalating cannibalistic/possessive enthusiasm ('I get the head! I love the brain in there!') goes from flirtatious to genuinely disturbing in rapid escalation
jokes.explanation: Ted's character escalation into bizarre possessiveness ('I love the brain in there') is funny and slightly menacing. The 'Arr, arr, arr' piratical enthusiasm is a good character quirk that makes this law firm feel appropriately predatory.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Thompson is the one who turned you in, Jeff. He went straight to the Dean.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? Why would Thompson do that?

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Because he's jealous of you. He's always been jealous.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Alan, that doesn't make any sense.

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: And another thing — Thompson has been acting really suspicious lately. Very suspicious. Have you noticed how suspicious he's been?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No...

dialogue.speaker: Alan
dialogue.line: Exactly! Because he doesn't want you to notice. Also, his wife left him last year. Or did she? Nobody's seen her since Thompson 'allegedly' went to the store for milk.

jokes.text: Um, checking in for the Heather pop and locklears. / Okay. And, um... Where's the rest of your team? / Oh, they'll be here. / I suppose you're allowed to start by yourself, but you won't stand a chance if you don't have someone... / They'll be here!
jokes.setup: Troy shows up to the pop-and-lock contest alone
jokes.punchline: Troy's increasingly desperate insistence ('They'll be here!') as the official grows more sympathetic and the situation more hopeless is a cringe comedy beat
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe beat. The repeated 'They'll be here!' with escalating desperation is a recognizable awkward situation played well, though not especially original.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: My feet are killing me! I've been dancing for hours!

dialogue.speaker: Announcer
dialogue.line: Have you tried just... not doing the moves that hurt?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Why didn't I think of that?

jokes.text: I brought stuff people use for capers. / Suction cup. / Credit card. / Chloroform.
jokes.setup: Annie presents her caper toolkit
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from benign (suction cup) to concerning (credit card) to genuinely alarming (chloroform) — with Annie delivering all three with equal matter-of-factness
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalating list structure builds to 'chloroform' as a perfect dark-subversive reveal from Annie — a character coded as goody-two-shoes. The equal deadpan delivery across all three items makes it funnier than any dramatic pause would. Character integration is very high — this is the first sign of 'dark Annie,' a recurring comedic vein. 'The credit card doesn't work, the chloroform does' as a follow-up is equally good.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I can't do this anymore. Not because of the dance contest. Because Jeff's leaving and I don't know how to be here without him.

jokes.text: The credit card doesn't work, the chloroform does.
jokes.setup: Annie listed suction cup, credit card, and chloroform as her toolkit
jokes.punchline: The evaluation of which tools work ('credit card doesn't, chloroform does') implies Annie has tested these — the casual admission of chloroform expertise from a college student is the horror/comedy
jokes.explanation: Possibly the episode's single best line. The parallel structure ('credit card doesn't work, the chloroform does') is a perfect delivery — clinical, matter-of-fact, devastating. Annie's dark competence with sedatives as a college girl is both wrong and hilarious. The economy is near-perfect. This line alone would justify the episode's reputation.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I didn't confront Alan. I have a better plan. I'm going to use him.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Use him how?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm going to befriend him, gain his trust, and then when he least expects it, I'll destroy him emotionally and intellectually.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's your better plan?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's a classic manipulation tactic. Works every time.

jokes.text: Annie, go back and keep lookout. / Why me lookout? Why not you guys? / 'Cause if someone comes up here, Kanye and Kumar get taken to jail. You get taken to dinner.
jokes.setup: The group divides roles for the office break-in
jokes.punchline: Abed's explanation — that Annie's white female presentation means she gets taken to dinner while Kanye (Troy) and Kumar (?) get taken to jail — is a sharp race-and-gender joke delivered with Abed's clinical detachment
jokes.explanation: Smart social commentary delivered as pure logistics. Abed's clinical framing of systemic racism/sexism as a practical caper-planning consideration is both uncomfortable and extremely funny. 'Kanye and Kumar' as the character nicknames is also a good quick joke. The delivery (Abed states it as obvious fact) is what elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Announcer
dialogue.line: And our final contestant is Jeff Winger!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, I can still enter? Awesome!

dialogue.speaker: Announcer
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, you need to have registered by 5 PM.

dialogue.speaker: Announcer
dialogue.line: Disqualified.

jokes.text: I am the smartest one in this whole group, and all I've been used for is bait and distraction.
jokes.setup: Annie is offended by being assigned lookout duty
jokes.punchline: Her complaint — that being smart hasn't saved her from being used as attractive bait — is both funny and genuinely a valid grievance, delivered with full Annie self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Good character joke with real bite. Annie's self-aware complaint about her role in the group has comedic truth — she IS the smartest and she IS constantly used for distraction. The mixture of pride and genuine grievance is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: No! No, no, no, no, NO! Do you understand what I've sacrificed?! Hours! HOURS of dancing! My feet are bleeding, my legs are numb, and for what?! For NOTHING?!

jokes.text: What did she say? / I don't know. All I heard was suck.
jokes.setup: Annie storms off saying 'I hope it sucks'
jokes.punchline: Troy's admission that he only heard 'suck' — either mishearing or only catching the most provocative word — is a funny reaction beat
jokes.explanation: Quick Troy/Abed beat. Troy's selective hearing of 'suck' is a mild laugh — the adolescent fixation on suggestive words is in character for Troy but not especially deep.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what? I've been thinking about what really matters in life, and it's friendship. Real, genuine friendship. And Chang, I want you to know that I consider you a true friend.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Really? Jeff, that means so much to me.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, but actually, looking back at our original agreement from three years ago, friendship was specifically defined as excluding anyone with a restraining order, which you currently have against the library. So technically, we're not friends.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: What? No!

jokes.text: He's a spineless trust fund jagoff.
jokes.setup: Ted privately reveals his real opinion of Alan to Jeff
jokes.punchline: 'Spineless trust fund jagoff' as the precise, specific characterization from someone who barely knows Alan on paper but has clearly assessed him deeply
jokes.explanation: Character-revealing insult. 'Jagoff' is a regionalism that suits Ted's character. The bluntness after Alan's self-important introduction is a good deflation.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Friendship is what really matters. We're a study group, a family. That's more important than any silly competition.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Now, according to the official rules, that means you're all disqualified for emotional manipulation.

jokes.text: Well, I only ever really liked one person. My mom. / And she liked my dad.
jokes.setup: Ted challenges Jeff to prove he actually likes Alan
jokes.punchline: Jeff's confession that he only ever liked his mom — immediately complicated by 'and she liked my dad' — reveals a lonely emotional backstory disguised as a punchline
jokes.explanation: Funny-sad joke. The admission ('I only ever really liked one person: my mom') already has tragic-comic energy, and the follow-up ('she liked my dad') efficiently explains the childhood wound while still being a joke. Character integration is high — this is the Jeff backstory that runs through the series.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm going to step through this painted tunnel now. According to the laws of cartoon physics, if there's no road ahead, I won't fall until I look down.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Abed, that's not how physics works.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Exactly. It's how cartoon physics works. There's a difference.

jokes.text: The student has become the master.
jokes.setup: Jeff delivers a perfect case for making Alan partner
jokes.punchline: Ted's 'the student has become the master' — clichéd martial arts movie language applied to lawyerly manipulation — is ironic both because Jeff is literally a student at community college and because the 'wisdom' is about being cynically good at manipulation
jokes.explanation: The literal irony of 'student becomes master' when Jeff is a literal student at community college is a decent quick joke. Not particularly fresh as a phrase but the context redeems it.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: If you just believe in cartoon physics, the tunnel will work.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I don't believe in cartoon physics.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Well, that might be why the tunnel didn't work.

jokes.text: Thank you, Jeff. You make me wanna be a worse man.
jokes.setup: Ted is inspired by Jeff's argument for making Alan partner
jokes.punchline: The standard 'you make me want to be a better man' compliment is inverted — the speech inspired him toward moral degradation, delivered as a sincere compliment
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The inversion of 'you make me want to be a better man' is structurally elegant and the specificity ('worse man') is perfect. Delivered as a genuine compliment by Ted, which makes it funnier. This is exactly the dark moral world these characters inhabit. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Did you know that if I sleep with Philip once a month, I can use his beach house in Rio whenever I want?
jokes.setup: Jeff is socializing at the party
jokes.punchline: The cheerful matter-of-fact disclosure that she has a transactional sexual arrangement for real estate access — 'I think you found the world's newest profession'
jokes.explanation: Good dark observation about the law firm's moral ecosystem. The cheerful disclosure sets up Jeff's response well.

jokes.text: You guys are really on to something. I think you found the world's newest profession.
jokes.setup: A female lawyer describes her monthly sex-for-Rio arrangement
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'world's newest profession' is a pointed ironic reversal — implying it's actually the world's OLDEST profession
jokes.explanation: Classic oldest-profession joke delivered with Jeff's signature ironic detachment. Familiar concept but efficiently executed.

jokes.text: Guys, guys, did you know I actually have a civil case against that bitch that stole my husband? / Shirley, don't sue a stripper. / Why not? / She's a stripper. Life sued her, and she lost.
jokes.setup: Shirley has apparently been socializing with lawyers and has a new idea
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'Life sued her, and she lost' — the metaphor of life as a litigant rendering summary judgment against a stripper — is both compassionate and perfectly cynical
jokes.explanation: 'Life sued her, and she lost' is a beautiful line — it uses legal language as existential poetry. The 'don't sue a stripper' advice is delivered with equal parts compassion and cynicism. The setup (Shirley enthusiastically pursuing legal vengeance) and Jeff's response (defending the stripper on practical/moral grounds) is a great character reversal.

jokes.text: Did you know there's an island in Indonesia where you can hunt people?
jokes.setup: Pierce has been wandering the party and returns with information
jokes.punchline: His excited discovery is about human hunting — which both fits Pierce's obliviousness and implies he found this appealing or useful
jokes.explanation: Perfect Pierce line. His enthusiasm for human hunting, delivered as a fun party fact, is exactly his character — oblivious to social norms, possibly dangerous, definitely a certain age and worldview. The Most Dangerous Game reference adds a layer.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! / I didn't know what to do. / I usually have one foot out of reality, and even I'm freaking out right now.
jokes.setup: Annie has chloroformed the janitor
jokes.punchline: Abed's 'I usually have one foot out of reality, and even I'm freaking out right now' — his self-aware commentary on his own dissociation from reality as a measure of how bad this is
jokes.explanation: Very strong Abed joke. His clinical self-description ('one foot out of reality') as a measuring stick for how alarming something is uses his meta-awareness as comedy. The implication is that for Abed to react emotionally, something has to be genuinely abnormal. Character integration is near-perfect.

jokes.text: You chloroformed the janitor? / Stop yelling at me! You're the ones that got caught! / You're the one who's yelling!
jokes.setup: Annie chloroformed an innocent janitor to escape detection
jokes.punchline: Annie's defensive pivot ('You're the ones that got caught!') shifts blame absurdly — getting caught is somehow the worse crime than chloroforming a janitor
jokes.explanation: Good escalating argument. Annie's self-righteous pivot to blame others for getting caught while she chloroformed an innocent person is a perfect Annie character moment.

jokes.text: Oh! Oh oh oh! / Guys, guys, guys! / Hey, hey, I have an idea. / Okay, it may sound a little weird, but trust me.
jokes.setup: The group is panicking about the chloroformed janitor
jokes.punchline: Annie's 'it may sound a little weird, but trust me' — coming from someone who just chloroformed an innocent person — is the highest possible red-flag preamble
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the group chloroform scheme. The 'it may sound a little weird, but trust me' from the person who already crossed the most extreme line is a solid ironic beat.

jokes.text: What's...Happening? / Oh! We all got chloroformed! / Somebody chloroformed all of us. / And now we're regaining consciousness together.
jokes.setup: Annie's plan involves chloroforming everyone to create plausible deniability
jokes.punchline: Abed narrates the group regaining consciousness as if it's a normal situation — 'And now we're regaining consciousness together' — his documentary-style commentary on waking up from chloroform is delivered with complete calm
jokes.explanation: Brilliant comedic payoff to the chloroform bit. Abed's narration of their own chloroforming ('And now we're regaining consciousness together') is delivered as if he's the documentary voice-over, which is both meta and deeply funny. The group chloroform plan is an inspired dark-absurdist escalation. 'I don't understand. Who's she?' followed by the rag-holding janitor is a perfect visual close.

jokes.text: I don't understand. Who's she? / (janitor is holding a rag)
jokes.setup: Everyone regains consciousness from chloroform
jokes.punchline: The janitor is holding the rag (the tool Annie used to chloroform them all) — the visual of the confused victim as the apparent perpetrator is the joke
jokes.explanation: Visual gag that works perfectly. The innocent janitor holding the rag in confusion while the group asks 'who's she?' creates the exact misidentification Annie intended — but we see it from the outside as absurdity. The timing implied by the transcript ('Why is she holding a rag?') completes the gag.

jokes.text: Okay, that was the worst idea ever. / Can we please just run away now? / Yeah. Yeah.
jokes.setup: The group has just woken up from Annie's chloroform plan
jokes.punchline: The cheerful consensus to 'just run away now' — combined with Abed's clinical verdict of 'worst idea ever' — is a good anticlimax
jokes.explanation: Minor button to the chloroform sequence. 'Can we please just run away now?' is a good deflating choice but the setup carries more weight than this close.

jokes.text: It is the fourth straight hour, and Ben Chang is still on his own.
jokes.setup: Ben Chang entered the pop-and-lock contest alone and has been competing for four hours
jokes.punchline: The sports-announcer framing applied to a community college break-dance contest, combined with Chang's inexplicable endurance as a solo competitor
jokes.explanation: Good Chang bit. The sports-announcer register applied to a Greendale dance contest is funny, and 'four straight hours' implies a level of deranged dedication that is entirely consistent with Chang's character.

jokes.text: My body hurts.
jokes.setup: Chang has been dancing for four-plus hours alone
jokes.punchline: The simple, pained confession — 'My body hurts' — is delivered mid-performance, implying he will continue despite the pain
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words that capture Chang's derangement. The implication that he will not stop despite physical pain is entirely consistent with his character.

jokes.text: You jealous because we're fitting in with your cool friends? / No. I'm distracted, watching you mutate.
jokes.setup: The study group has been enthusiastically fitting into the law firm culture
jokes.punchline: 'Watching you mutate' as the description — not 'change' or 'grow' but 'mutate' — implies the transformation is deformative rather than positive
jokes.explanation: 'Mutate' is a precise and funny word choice — it implies biological deformity rather than social growth, which suits Jeff's clinical-but-caring observation style. Good line.

jokes.text: Britta, you're not a whore. / Shirley, Jesus turned the other cheek. He didn't garnish wages. / Pierce, do I even need to say this? / It is bad to hunt man for sport. / Bad ass.
jokes.setup: Jeff is correcting each group member's behavior at the law firm party
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from 'you're not a whore' to 'don't garnish wages' to 'don't hunt man for sport' — each correction implies a worse transgression. Pierce's 'Bad ass' response is the button.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's structural highlights. The escalating list of corrections — each revealing a worse group member behavior — builds to 'it is bad to hunt man for sport' as the peak absurdity. Pierce's 'Bad ass' (hearing his correction as a compliment) is a perfect character button. The list structure is clean, the escalation is precise, and the character integration across all three corrections is excellent.

jokes.text: He stabbed you in the back, Jeff. He's a bad friend.
jokes.setup: The group has found the email proving Alan turned Jeff in
jokes.punchline: Abed's reduction of a years-long betrayal that derailed Jeff's career to 'He's a bad friend' is both clinically reductive and emotionally accurate from Abed's perspective
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed reductionism. His translation of a major life-betrayal into 'bad friend' is simultaneously the least and most important thing that could be said. The simplicity is the joke and the character truth.

jokes.text: You're right. He is a bad friend. / But he is a good lawyer.
jokes.setup: Jeff acknowledges the betrayal
jokes.punchline: His pivot — agreeing on 'bad friend' but immediately separating 'good lawyer' as the more important quality — reveals Jeff's value system with both comedy and pathos
jokes.explanation: Very well-structured character beat. The parallel concession/pivot ('bad friend / good lawyer') uses Jeff's lawyer logic against human decency. The comedic economy is excellent — it's two short sentences that reveal the whole character.

jokes.text: Would you stop? / Tango! / I don't know how you did it, man, but you're looking at the firm's next partner. / If I wasn't actively repressing my bi-curiosity, I would kiss you full on your beautiful mouth.
jokes.setup: Alan thanks Jeff for getting him the partnership
jokes.punchline: 'If I wasn't actively repressing my bi-curiosity' as a qualifier — which is a funny overshare that also implies the repression is an ongoing active process rather than a resolved matter
jokes.explanation: 'Actively repressing my bi-curiosity' as a continuous present-tense action is a funny construction. The specificity of 'bi-curiosity' rather than something blunter shows some care in the word choice.

jokes.text: You probably know that it was someone here at the firm who turned you in.
jokes.setup: Jeff sets up Alan for a confession
jokes.punchline: The phrasing 'you probably know' implies Jeff is testing whether Alan will volunteer the information — the meta-manipulation is happening in real time
jokes.explanation: Decent beat, more dramatic than comedic. The setup for Jeff's manipulation of Alan.

jokes.text: It was Thompson. / Thompson that adopted three at-risk teens and donated his kidney to a temp. / All an act. / Why do you think he quit right after you left? / Well, his... his wife died. / Did she... Jeff? / Did... She?
jokes.setup: Alan blames Jeff's disbarment on 'Thompson,' and Jeff begins dismantling the alibi
jokes.punchline: 'Well, his wife died. / Did she... Jeff? / Did... She?' — Alan implying Thompson might have killed his wife, delivered with chilling casualness, then Jeff's dawning realization creates dark comedic horror
jokes.explanation: Very well-structured dark sequence. The escalation from 'he ratted on you' to 'he killed his wife?' lands because Alan keeps raising the stakes while trying to deflect blame. 'Did she... Jeff? Did... She?' is a brilliantly uncomfortable callback structure — Alan pausing to let the implication land is creepy-funny. The good-character setup ('adopted at-risk teens, donated kidney to a temp') makes the pivot darker.

jokes.text: Hey, let's go do some shots with Phil, huh? / No, you go ahead. I, uh... / I think I caught something... at... at Greendale. / College chicks. I get ya! / You're bad!
jokes.setup: Jeff uses 'catching something at Greendale' as his excuse to leave
jokes.punchline: Ted interprets 'caught something at Greendale' as a sexually transmitted implication from 'college chicks' — the misread being exactly the wrong kind of community college reputation
jokes.explanation: Decent misreading joke. Ted's 'College chicks. I get ya!' is a funny and entirely wrong interpretation. The irony that Jeff has 'caught' genuine human connection at Greendale makes it land thematically too.

jokes.text: It hurts! / Shamone...It hurts! / Ben, you need to switch up your moves.
jokes.setup: Chang has been dancing for over five hours
jokes.punchline: 'Shamone' as a Michael Jackson reference mid-agony, combined with the practical advice to 'switch up your moves' as if that will address five hours of physical torment
jokes.explanation: Good Chang continuation. 'Shamone...It hurts!' using Michael Jackson's vocalization (episode aired 2010, one year post-MJ death) while expressing genuine agony is a funny mix. The practical advice ('switch up your moves') is hilariously beside the point.

jokes.text: oh! / Only two teams left. The poppy lockstockings, and the Heather pop and locklears!
jokes.setup: The pop-and-lock contest has been running for hours
jokes.punchline: The team names — 'Poppy Lockstockings' (Pippi Longstocking + pop-lock) and 'Heather Pop and Locklears' (Heather Locklear + pop-lock) — are groan-worthy celebrity puns deployed with straight-announcer energy
jokes.explanation: Fun wordplay. Both puns ('Poppy Lockstockings' and 'Heather Pop and Locklears') are well-constructed and the contrast between children's literature and 80s TV celebrity is amusing.

jokes.text: Jeffrey, did you punch Alan in his rotten face and then storm out? / Hell, no. That guy's useful to me.
jokes.setup: Jeff returns to the pop-and-lock contest
jokes.punchline: Shirley hopes for satisfying revenge; Jeff's response is the opposite — Alan's usefulness as leverage is what Jeff values, not justice
jokes.explanation: Very Jeff. The refusal of emotional satisfaction in favor of strategic positioning ('that guy's useful to me') is both funny and character-perfect. Shirley's setup (hoping for punching) is a great contrast.

jokes.text: Thanks to you, I've now got leverage over a spineless jag that just made partner. That is the place I want to work. But I prefer to hang out with cool people, people so cool... they care.
jokes.setup: Jeff explains his decision to stay at Greendale
jokes.punchline: 'People so cool... they care' — the ultimate inversion of Jeff's earlier dismissal ('caring is lethal'), delivered as a speech that the group has been waiting for but undercut by Jeff's own awareness that it's slightly cheesy
jokes.explanation: Jeff's character arc wrapped into a line. 'People so cool they care' as an inversion of his earlier 'caring is lethal' is structurally complete, though it verges more on sincerity than comedy. The slight self-consciousness in the delivery saves it.

jokes.text: And now...The puppet.
jokes.setup: Jeff has just given his cool speech and joined the dance
