jokes.punchline: 'And now...The puppet.' — implying a specific dance move has been withheld for this moment — the anticipation built by the phrasing versus the mundane-sounding move name
jokes.explanation: Good economy. 'And now...The puppet.' as a dramatic announcement for a pop-and-lock move is funny in its self-seriousness. The audience imagines whatever 'the puppet' looks like, which is probably funnier than showing it.

jokes.text: Ah, no parking on the dance floor, Winger. / No, I'm serious. You're disqualified. / The winners are the poppy lockstockings!
jokes.setup: Jeff dramatically joins the dance as the climax
jokes.punchline: He is immediately disqualified — his triumphant entrance accomplishes nothing and his team loses anyway
jokes.explanation: Perfect anticlimactic structure. The whole arc — missing the contest, big speech, dramatic entrance — ends in immediate disqualification. The deflation of narrative expectation is well-executed and consistent with Community's structure-subverting ethos.

jokes.text: Noooooo! / I been popping and locking for five hours, and you threw it all away! / The contest doesn't matter. What's important is we have each other.
jokes.setup: The group loses the contest due to Jeff's late entry
jokes.punchline: Chang's anguished 'Noooooo!' after five hours of solo dancing — his investment in the contest vastly exceeds anyone else's — contrasted immediately with the group's warm 'what matters is we have each other'
jokes.explanation: Chang's breakdown is the perfect payoff for his five-hour subplot. His devastation is proportionate to his insane investment, and the heartwarming group speech that immediately follows makes his grief funnier by ignoring it. The juxtaposition is classic Community structure.

jokes.text: That was dope, what we did. That was so good! / The puppet too! The puppet was so... / I rolled my ankle during that. / Aw! Twisted it? / It was worth it, though.
jokes.setup: The group celebrates their failed-but-spirited performance
jokes.punchline: Jeff's admission that 'the puppet' caused an injury — but that it was 'worth it' — is a funny self-undermining callback. The group's enthusiasm in the face of losing is the larger joke.
jokes.explanation: Warm tag scene. 'The puppet was so...' trailing off before Jeff reveals an ankle injury is a nice beat. 'It was worth it, though' is a good closer for the puppt gag.

jokes.text: You know what, he's bringing us down. Let's move him. Can we move him?
jokes.setup: Chang is sulking about the loss while the group celebrates
jokes.punchline: Troy treats Chang like an object to be repositioned — 'Can we move him?' as a practical solution to his emotional state
jokes.explanation: Good Troy joke. His practical 'can we move him?' solution to emotional discomfort is very Troy — physical problem-solving for emotional situations. The word choice ('bringing us down' as spatial rather than emotional) is funny.

jokes.text: Psst! Troy! It's me. Abed? / I made it through! / I'm a cartoon now.
jokes.setup: Earlier in the episode Abed said he painted a tunnel on the library wall and was going to run through it
jokes.punchline: He appears to have done it — he is now 'a cartoon' — delivered with complete sincerity as a payoff to the episode's most absurdist setup
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the best payoffs in the series. The setup at 01:03 is 20 minutes earlier — a throwaway Abed line about a painted Looney Tunes tunnel. The payoff: Abed appears behind a wall ('Psst! Troy!') and announces 'I'm a cartoon now.' The joke works on three levels: (1) pure absurdism — he genuinely believes/exists in cartoon logic; (2) meta-commentary on Community's escalating surrealism (callbacks to the cartoonish campus); (3) character perfection — Abed is the ONLY character this works for. The structure across a full episode is extraordinary. This earns high craft scores because the construction is genuinely exceptional, not just funny in the moment.

jokes.text: That's impossible. / Nothing's impossible in here. Animals can talk. Your heart is shaped like a heart. And the smell of pie can make you float.
jokes.setup: Abed announces he is now a cartoon
jokes.punchline: His description of cartoon physics — 'your heart is shaped like a heart / the smell of pie can make you float' — delivered as genuine selling points for cartoon existence
jokes.explanation: Brilliant follow-through. The list of cartoon physics — 'animals can talk / your heart is shaped like a heart / the smell of pie can make you float' — is inventive and funny on its own, but 'your heart is shaped like a heart' is the genuine standout: an observation that makes no sense in reality but is exactly how cartoon hearts work. 'The smell of pie can make you float' is a perfect Proustian/cartoon combination. Each item in the list is genuinely original. This may be a stronger individual joke than the setup.

jokes.text: You have to believe, Troy. / Wait! You don't have to believe. / I didn't.
jokes.setup: Abed encourages Troy to believe to join cartoon world
jokes.punchline: He immediately corrects himself — 'You don't have to believe. I didn't.' — which both undermines the inspirational movie trope AND implies Abed entered cartoon reality through pure mechanistic action rather than faith
jokes.explanation: Perfect closer for the episode's best bit. The self-correction ('Wait! You don't have to believe. I didn't.') subverts the inspirational-movie 'you have to believe' trope while simultaneously being a profound Abed character statement — he didn't believe in cartoon logic, he just ACTED on it. The implication that reality responds to behavior rather than faith is both funny and weirdly philosophical. Maximum economy — the punch is in the last three words. This is exceptional writing.

jokes.text: I may have done some damage there.
jokes.setup: Abed has just delivered the cartoon-world pitch to Troy
jokes.punchline: His quiet aside — 'I may have done some damage there' — implies awareness that his cartoon-physics description may have destabilized Troy's grip on reality, delivered with complete calm
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the entire episode's best bit. Abed's completely calm self-assessment of potential psychological damage — delivered as a mild regret — is funny because he's right, and because his response to causing existential damage is 'I may have done some damage there' rather than any concern. Character integration is near-perfect.

tmdb_overview: When an old friend from Jeff's past appears unexpectedly, his friends discover that he was the one responsible for Jeff's disbarment.
insight: Absurdist lawyer comedy sustains 3.5 jokes per minute across 75 total jokes.
